subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF LICENSING OF LIVE ORAL POLIO VACCINE

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monleiih (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF LICENSING OF LIVE ORAL POLIO VACCINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that live oral polio virus vaccine of the Sabin variety has now been licensed under the Food and Drugs Act for use in Canada.
This new vaccine represents another great medical breakthrough and one which may in effect result in the almost complete eradication of paralytic polio in this country. I know that hon. members will take satisfaction, as I do, in the fact that Canada is among the first nations of the world to license all three strains of the vaccine. Our regulations in this regard set a very high standard, and I think it is a tribute to the excellence of Canadian scientists and Canadian producers that full approval has now been possible.
I might say we have taken this step only after long and careful study. There are many special problems associated with a vaccine of this type, and considerable time has been required to solve them. In addition to the information provided by research and field trials in other countries, a good deal of work has been done in Canada, in Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The results of these efforts have confirmed that the Sabin strains of live oral polio virus vaccine are safe for community use in Canada and that they are also valuable immunizing agents.
Because of the really outstanding success achieved with the Salk vaccine and because it is now built into child immunization programs across the country, we do not expect that the oral vaccine will replace the Salk at least at the outset. Rather it will be used as a supplementary or booster dose for the majority of persons who already have been immunized with the Salk, as well as for a primary stimulus for those who have not. In the case of immunized persons, the initial approach is that a single dose of the oral vaccine will be sufficient. Several doses may be necessary for those not previously immunized with Salk.
I might add that evidence to date suggests that the most effective method of using oral vaccine in our present state of knowledge is by community immunization programs. For this reason, and in order to make the best possible use of supplies available, distribution for the time being will be through provincial and federal health authorities.
As in the case of the Salk vaccine, the costs of providing the Sabin vaccine will be shared on a fifty-fifty basis by the federal and provincial governments. Also as was done with the Salk, production in Canada will be handled by the Connaught medical research laboratories of the University of Toronto and the institute of microbiology and hygiene of the University of Montreal.
As I have mentioned, careful preparation has been made for the use of this new weapon against polio, and in view of this I have every confidence that we will achieve a record with the Sabin vaccine that will match our outstanding success with the Salk vaccine in terms of safety and effectiveness.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF LICENSING OF LIVE ORAL POLIO VACCINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there will be general satisfaction in the house and throughout the country with the announcement that the department has decided to license three strains of the vaccine of the Sabin variety, which is to be orally administered. It is interesting to note that this does not mean the replacement of the Salk vaccine, in the initial stages at any rate.
It is also a matter of satisfaction that the Connaught laboratories at the University of Toronto and the institute of microbiology at the University of Montreal, under Dr. Armand Frappier, will continue to provide the production of this new orally administered vaccine as they did in the case of the Salk vaccine.
The minister, however, has said nothing about the tests to be employed both at the Connaught laboratories and at the institute of microbiology, as well as in the department here in Ottawa, to make sure that doses of this vaccine meet the standards of safety laid down by the Department of National Health and Welfare in co-operation with the provincial departments of health. The minister will recall that in the case of the Salk vaccine, Canada was privileged to escape some of the abuses and dangers which attended the administration of Salk vaccine in the United States because of the great care which was taken in Canada in testing various batches of the Salk vaccine.

Inquiries of the Ministry
I hope the minister can give the house some assurance that every possible device will be employed in Canada to make sure that doses of this vaccine in this country are tested by the production centres as well as by the department's laboratory here in Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, concerning the resolution put forward by the Minister of Finance to extend the loan period in the Farm Improvement Loans Act, there are just a few words I should like to say.
The measure has nothing new to offer. Its purpose is simply to extend the period for making loans from July 1, 1962, to June 30, 1965, and to increase the limit of guaranteed loans to $400 million.
It does not bring any real change and contributes nothing to improve the farmer's lot. The situation, for the farmer, remains the same. Nothing is done to provide him with a better income for the good of his family.
Such is the policy of the present government, no general plan to improve conditions for the farmers. Since 1957, confusion has prevailed in our country's farm policy. There is no program, no planning.
The pamphlet called ARDA has often been mentioned. For the past four years, there has been some talk about the establishment of a food bank.

a great improvement over anything existing previously. There has been an improvement, but this improvement does not need to stop. Certainly if there was any foresight in the Conservative party they would be considering the extension of this particular act at this particular time, in addition to the increases that have taken place in the amount of money available over the period of years. I suggest that this should happen with regard to the maximum amount of money permitted to a particular farmer.
We endorse this type of legislation. We are very happy that it carries the present interest rate. We believe that this act has served a purpose. Certainly the Minister of Finance went to great lengths to point out this fact. I agree that it has done so, but I think now is the time to quit playing with this type of legislation and make it permanent. We amended this act in 1948, 1951, 1953 and in 1956, when we made an additional change by putting in $5,000 as the maximum allowable loan per farmer. In 1959 the act was again amended and the maximum amount was raised to $7,500.
When we are amending it now for a period from 1962 to 1965 I suggest that the minister should give some consideration to the farmers' request on numerous occasions to raise the maximum amount to $10,000. I make this suggestion because I think it is in keeping with the original concept of this act. Farmers at one time would consider $3,000 on a 10 year mortgage to be a sufficient amount of money.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GUARANTEE LOANS, ESTABLISH LIMITS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GUARANTEE LOANS, ESTABLISH LIMITS, ETC.

Yes, as the hon. member from Alberta mentioned, the machine companies would have considered it a suitable loan in 1948. But in 1962 I would ask the hon. member from Alberta this question. Farmers in his part of the country, as in other parts of Canada, must extend their operations and their capital expenditures. Is it possible for a farmer with $7,500 to go out and buy a new tractor and a new combine, or is it possible to buy either one for $7,500?
I suggest that the amount of money now available under this act is not sufficient. I think that statement applies to western Canada and also, though more recently, to the dairy industry in Ontario. That amount of $7,500 is not sufficient to buy a bulk tank and bulk cooler for handling whole milk in Ontario. A few years ago you could go out and for several thousand dollars could buy a cooler plus milking machines. It has become increasingly difficult to pick up for
Farm Improvement Loans Act $7,500 a bulk cooler and the tanks and the piping that are necessary. I think it is impossible to do so.
I therefore suggest that if the minister is being progressive he will consider increasing the amount. Oh, there is one member who says it is not true. This may be so. He may rise in his place and say it is not true, if he wishes to do so. He may even point out that $3,000 was too much for the farmer to be able to borrow in 1948. But I think it certainly was not more in 1948 at $3,000 than it is now when we allow $7,500. I suggest that the maximum amount should be $10,000. I should hasten to add that most of the farmers will not borrow $10,000. They are very good businessmen and they know, as the Household Finance people tell the Canadian public, that one should never borrow needlessly. It is foolish to borrow money when you are not obliged to do so. I think the farmer has always been in this position. He is not going to borrow money except when it is absolutely necessary in order that he may stay in business; and in some cases it is going to be necessary to have more money available than $7,500 under this particular act.
There is one last point I wish to make, Mr. Chairman. I would think the minister should give some consideration at this time to the necessary amendment in order to permit farmers to combine to buy farm machinery. This would mean they could get together and co-operate in securing the machinery necessary for their operations. The remarks of the hon. member for Roberval demand that the problem posed by this bill be shown in better perspective. I refer to the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, better known as the Gordon report, which points out that farm output between 1935-39


and 1940-1944 increased by some 30 per cent as a result of much more intensive cultivation. The rapid mechanization of Canadian agriculture since the end of the war has involved larger cash outlays for a great many things, particularly machinery, and there has been a considerable technological revolution in farming, with heavier purchases of commercial feeds, seeds and fertilizers. This has resulted in a substantially increased capital structure on even the small farm. The commission found that in every province farming had become much more highly capitalized and that the capital is increasingly concentrated in machinery, implements and livestock rather than in land and buildings.
This is the most spectacular change we have seen in Canadian agriculture. The mechanical revolution has come to the farm and made a great many changes. This has been so in all walks of Canadian life and it is certainly so even in eastern agriculture, the depressed area of agriculture today. The Gordon commission said it appears likely that the technological changes of most importance over the next 25 years will be those designed primarily to increase the productivity of nature rather than the productivity of labour. It will be seen that much mechanical equipment has gone on to the farms; that there is less labour used, while the units of land are larger. There has been a rapid trend toward fewer farms, and this trend is likely to continue. The commission came to the conclusion that the number of farms in Canada, which in 1951 numbered 623,000, might decline to
570,000	by 1965 and to 540,000 by 1980. The conclusion was reached that the size of the average farm in 1980 would be 326 acres compared with an average size of 279 acres in 1951.
Following this study which, the committee will remember, took place in 1956, the chairman of that commission, Mr. Walter L. Gordon, wrote a book called "Troubled Canada". In it he said that in the ten years since 1950 employment in agriculture had dropped by one third. He concluded that the agricultural industry was going through a period of drastic change amounting almost to a revolution. He says it is important that this transformation be as gradual as possible and that it should be facilitated by capital changes whenever this can be done, so that the hardships that are bound to occur when people leave the land may be eased to the greatest extent of which we are capable.
The really serious problem is this. As these farmers across Canada are readjusting themselves to an extent never known before in our agricultural experience, they are caught by the squeeze between the rising prices

they must pay for the goods they require and the falling prices received for the goods they have to sell.

Mr. Chairman, I hope to draw my remarks to an early conclusion. At precisely the moment of change to which I referred the cost-price squeeze is more significant than ever before. The index of farm prices of agricultural products stood at 231.3 during 1956 as compared with 243.3 during 1961. This represents an increase of approximately 5 per cent in the prices received by farmers from the sale of their products. On the other hand, the price index of commodities and services used by farmers increased from 230.3 in 1956 to 258.3 in 1961, or by about 12 per cent. Thus while the price of products sold by farmers increased by only 5 per cent, the prices of products bought by farmers used in production increased by 12 per cent. The farmer's costs have thus gone up twice as fast as the prices he receives.
The problem of the rising prices of machinery and other farm costs is sufficiently serious that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture as recently as February 7, 1962 made the following submission to the government:
Farm improvement loans.
In view of rising prices of machinery and other farm costs, and the continuing technological advance that is increasing the capital investment in machinery and equipment needed for efficient farming, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture believes the present loan limit for farm improvement loans of $7,500 should be raised, perhaps to $10,000. The raising of the maximum loan limit

Farm Improvement Loans Act only makes possible such loans where they are reasonable and necessary for good farm business and investment practice.
A valuable study group called the Ontario farmer-labour conference met at Port Elgin on June 18-19, 1960, comprising representatives of labour and farm organizations. One of the guest speakers was Hon. W. A. Good-fellow, minister of agriculture for Ontario. I was impressed by his remarks, which are set out in the report of the conference at page 35. Referring to farm production Mr. Good-fellow said:
But in spite of the fact that we have a much smaller area in production, we are producing approximately 34 per cent more than we did in 1946. From 1941-1956, the number of Ontario farms reporting motor trucks and tractors nearly tripled. The number reporting grain combines increased 20 times. At the same time 38,000 farms had ceased to operate in the province of Ontario. Those are rather revealing figures. In 1900 a farmer fed, including his own family, nine people. A farmer in the province of Ontario this year through mechanized equipment, better farm management, better productive methods, will feed approximately 36 people
This illustrates the startling change to which I have referred. An interesting study of the province of Ontario is reported in the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce commercial letter No. 2 of February, 1962. Referring to the situation of Ontario farmers the report states:
Coincident with the rising production of Ontario farmers there has been a gradual decline in the total farm acreage and in the number of farms, and a fairly marked increase in the average size of holding.
The report goes on to speak of the improvements technology has made possible and the decreased labour requirements. These factors have left a large problem. That is, how is the farmer, particularly the farmer in the east, going to survive? As a previous speaker on this side has indicated, it is not good enough for the government to assist only the farmer in the west.
The annual report for 1960 relating to the Farm Improvement Loans Act published by the Department of Finance contains some interesting figures in a table set out at page 13. The table reveals that there has been a decline in the number of people in the province of Ontario obtaining loans under this act from 12,874 in 1959 to 11,881 in 1960. The value of these loans in Ontario has declined from $19,109,964 in 1959 to $18,737,174 in 1960. In Ontario there has been a substantial drop both in the number of applications and in the amount of loans. There has been a substantial increase in the loans extended in the province of Saskatchewan, but in the national picture we find that in 1960 as compared with 1959 there has been an increase in the total amount of money lent under the act of less than

$3,500,000. It is difficult to examine those figures and have them make much sense in the light of the comments made by the hon. member for Roberval.

This debate has ranged far and wide, and I do not intend to contribute or add to your difficulties in trying to control it, Mr. Chairman. However, there are a few remarks I should like to make on this subject. The matter of farm credit is one that concerns all farmers. Being a farmer myself, this matter really concerns me. The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska talked about everything. He said specifically that he could talk about farm problems for two days. However, he failed to talk for one minute on this particular measure. Whether or not that fact was owing to some problem
Farm Improvement Loans Act he had in understanding it, I do not know. However, I tried desperately to gather some of the thoughts he might have on this particular resolution and failed to do so. Possibly it was my fault; I do not know.
The hon. member for Timiskaming stated that he thought the loan maximum should be increased in amount to $10,000, complained that the government was continually bringing in measures such as this one, and expressed the opinion that it should be put on the statute books permanently so that the money would be there whether the government appropriated it or not.
This measure is similar to others which have come before the house in past years. Its purpose is to establish $400 million as the limit of guaranteed loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Previously, the limit was $300 million. Actually last year $101 million were lent under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. We are again establishing the act to take effect from 1962 until 1965. One good reason for doing this is that if loans continue to be made at the rate at which they were made last year, namely at the rate of $101 million a year, for the next three years, they would possibly exceed the $300 million limit that was established under this act. We are therefore increasing it in order to allow farmers to borrow without any halt under this act for purposes which they feel are feasible.
With regard to the $10,000 limit placed on each farmer may I say this. Actually in the west today we are seeing a trend away from heavy capitalization of equipment. I firmly believe that most western members here will agree with me on this matter. Perhaps the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska and the hon. member for Timiskaming do not realize that fact. The farmers are looking around and are buying better combines that are not self-propelled. They are buying them with power take-offs. With the advent of the power take-off being a common thing in large tractors, farmers are going back to the power take-off combine rather than the self-propelled combine. Therefore 1 think it is quite feasible for a farmer to buy a new combine and a new tractor, provided he has some down payment; and most farmers are trading in a tractor. I think it is quite feasible for him to buy under the limit to which we have increased, namely $7,500. While there are no doubt a number of farmers who would like to see the limit established at an even higher figure, may I say that those are large farmers. As has been pointed out in this debate, the average loan under the Farm Improvement Loans Act is something like $1,497 or about $1,500. The average farmer would likely be paying on three or four loans

Farm Improvement Loans Act at one time. It has been customary for the banks in western Canada particularly to lend on a three year basis amounts under $4,000. If a farmer borrows more than $4,000 on a new combine, building, repairs or a new tractor, the banks generally try to work it out over five years and so on. The number of years bear a relationship to the amount of money lent. I feel, of course, that this bill which will increase the amount will have an effect and will allow the farmers to continue to borrow money.
We had from the hon. member for Fort William a talk with regard to farm credit. However, I think his whole speech dealt with the farm credit corporation rather than with this particular Farm Improvement Loans Act. I think there is evidence under that particular piece of legislation that this government is making major strides forward in increasing loans and in increasing the money available to farmers for the purpose of establishing themselves as an economic unit. I think the interesting thing about this particular measure and the operations under it last year is that 42 per cent of the borrowers obtained money for the first time under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. To me this is a very surprising thing. I was under the impression that most farmers in western Canada have been using this particular piece of legislation for years in order to buy their machinery. However, under last year's operation 42 per cent of the borrowers used this legislation for the first time. I think this is a very encouraging thing. This is a worth-while piece of legislation and one which will enable the farmers to become more mechanized at a reasonable cost to them.
Another very encouraging thing is that more farmers borrowed money last year under the Farm Improvement Loans Act in order to purchase livestock. Here again 1 think they are moving in the right direction.
The hon. member for Leeds made a scholarly speech about agriculture. He relied on some more of his scholarly colleagues to deal with the agriculture problem. I would suggest to him that if he relied on a few more farmers in the future, he might get the facts a little bit straighter. He discussed farm prices but I do not intend to go into that matter at all. However, he quoted some figures from the dominion bureau of statistics which are as yet not up to date. He was confused about table 13 in the annual report as to why Ontario farmers had taken out fewer loans this year and Saskatchewan farmers had taken out more loans than last year, and so on. This depends to a great extent on when the machinery wears out. I do not think we should encourage farmers to take loans unless

they need new machinery. It has been a common fault of a lot of farmers over the years to borrow money and buy new combines when it was questionable whether or not they needed to do so. Without a doubt the reason why Saskatchewan farmers borrowed more money last year by taking advantage of this legislation was the fact that the cycle of use of given machines was running out.
One can go back into the history of farm machinery purchases and see that in the case of the province of Saskatchewan 1952 and 1953 were heavy years with respect to the buying of machinery. This machinery has now lasted eight or nine years. It is wearing out and the farmers are purchasing similar machinery. That is why there were more loans in Saskatchewan last year than the previous year. I think the same thing may hold true for Ontario farmers who are no doubt operating on a somewhat different cycle.
The hon. member suggested at one time that farmers were not borrowing enough. He was disappointed that in Ontario loans had gone down by approximately $1 million. However, just before ending his speech he said that we cannot lend the farmers money thus increasing their debt and expect them to get out of their troubles. The hon. member left me confused with respect to whether he was in favour of more money for the farmers or less money for the farmers.
He spoke at some length about the dairy farmers in his area needing new milk plants and suggested that this would not increase their net earnings to any great extent. Certainly it would increase the efficiency of their dairy operations and this should be their guide in deciding whether or not they will take out loans. I sincerely support the resolution because I feel it is a very necessary one, having in mind the fact that farmers are taking advantage of this legislation in increasing numbers.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks I should like to make on this measure at this time. It is one of those measures that have come before parliament periodically throughout the years and it has been of very great benefit to the farmers of this country. It is a type of act that has been based on co-operation between the federal government and the chartered banks and it has been a very useful measure indeed. Farmers have obtained the necessary credit for many aspects of farming at a nominal rate of interest and the banks, encouraged by the government guarantee and by the present Minister of Finance and his predecessors, have been very active in the lending field.
When the act was first placed on the statute books in 1945 the maximum loan was $3,000.

Farm Improvement Loans Act I think it is correct to say that machines that could be purchased for a total of $3,000 in 1945 now cost very nearly $10,000. Today's machines may be somewhat larger and more efficient, but there has been a tremendous increase in the price of farm implements and I think the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has made a reasonable and sensible request, namely that the maximum be increased from $7,500 to $10,000.
Farmers have demonstrated that they are very excellent credit risks. Under the act they have borrowed more than $1 billion up to the end of 1960, the last year for which a report is available, and the claims paid by the government have amounted to only one tenth of one per cent. This demonstrates that farmers are a very good credit risk. I would hope that the minister will consider the suggestion of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Farmers are caught up in a very rapid technological revolution at the present time. The mechanization of farms is continuing at an ever accelerated rate. I think that to increase the maximum to $10,000 would merely recognize this existing fact.
I should like to ask the minister for some information if he has it, either at this stage or at a later stage, as to the number of repossessions of farm implements made under the act, the disposition of those farm implements and the personal claims on the borrowers following the disposal of these implements.

I was interested in the comments made by the hon. member for Acadia. I wonder if he has given consideration to the fact that money borrowed for the purpose of purchasing livestock, unless it is for breeding stock, is usually borrowed for a short period of time. I wonder if he has considered the fact that the $400 million available is to cover losses guaranteed by the government and the guarantee covers 10 per cent of the amount borrowed under this particular section.
In so far as farm machinery is concerned, the other day I inquired of a farm organization what they considered the average would be for loans under this act for the purchase of farm machinery. They were of the opinion it would be fair to say that the borrowing period would not be 10 years but would be somewhere between three and five years. Under normal circumstances, the farmer would be able to make repayment in that period of time. Obviously if a farmer were to use the loan for the purchase of livestock the period of the loan would not run to ten years but would probably be closer to three years. I would think, therefore, that the amount of money being borrowed would have very little relationship to the $400 million. In my opinion, it is not correct to say that the $400 million will be used up after three or more years because this year we will be using something over $100 million. I would suggest that, at the end of three years, most of this money will have been repaid and the banks will no longer be requesting the 10 per cent guarantee from the government. I suggest that if this is true, then the money can be used as a sort of revolving fund and the amount used would continue to average about $100 million a year.
If this is the case, perhaps the government should be asking for a larger sum of money now. When the minister replies, I think he should bear in mind what the hon. member for Acadia has said. What the hon. member has said may be true in western Canada where other factors are involved. If the loans are not repaid in the normal period of from three to five years, it may be necessary to have more money available. I know of a farmer in western Canada who has been looking for a sizeable amount of money with which to buy livestock. He has the opportunity of going into this business on a fairly large scale. His desire is to borrow the 

money for three years because, in his words, if he has not made it in three years then he will be carrying his cattle at a loss.
I would suggest that the minister give consideration to this, as well as to the other matters mentioned. I compliment the hon. member for Acadia upon his restraint in asking his own minister to meet this additional request. However, I certainly will make it on his behalf because of his modesty.

the second reading of Bill No. S-6, to incorporate Cochin Pipe Lines Ltd.
He said: Mr. Speaker, by this bill a group of Edmonton people ask parliament to incorporate them as a body for the purpose of undertaking a study and building a pipe line between the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I wish to assure the house that the owners of this company are all Edmonton residents and Canadian citizens. The pipe line company is going to be completely owned and built by Canadians, operated by Canadians, and in so far as forseeable plans are concerned it is strictly for carrying petroleum products between the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
At present the actual construction plans are not complete because in order to finalize their plans it is necessary to carry out a marketing and feasibility study. The pipe line will run roughly between the area of Hugh-enden, Alberta, and Melville, Saskatchewan, a distance of 300 or 400 miles. It will connect a couple of natural gas reservoirs, and it is intended that they should carry what are called the light ends of gas, the butane, propane-the l.p.g's in other words. The pipe line will not interfere or compete with any other existing pipe line.
The bill as it now stands is in the usual form, with the usual powers that a pipe line body seeks, including the power to export, because they feel that with the development of the uses of these types of gases and their marketing there may well come a day in the not too distant future when there may be a market in the northern part of the United States, and they would not want to come back to ask for that power if at that time it was found good business to go further.

I wish to point out to the house that before they could undertake the construction it would be necessary to have the approval of the conservation boards of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and that all this house is being asked to do is allow them to become a body which can invest the necessary moneys to carry out feasibility studies to see if they can do it, and to carry on further with their plans.
This bill will be referred to a committee and we will have the opportunity of questioning the proposed president of the company, and all technical questions will be answered at that time. I can answer a few of the questions, if any hon. member has any. I hope that the house will encourage these enterprising Canadians who are keeping Canadian money at home and putting it to work on Canadian products, which I think will greatly benefit our part of the country.

the second reading of Bill No. C-17, to amend the House of Commons Act (internal economy autonomy).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I mean nothing disrespectful to Your Honour by this, but I think it is a fact that, contrary to common

Private Bills
opinion and common understanding, you are not a free agent in the discharge of your duties and responsibilities, to the extent that you have along with you in the exercise of some of your duties a number of ministers of the crown who participate with you in coming to some decisions.
The house and its environs are supposed to be under your authority Mr. Speaker, but I submit that by virtue of the House of Commons Act which this bill seeks to amend, such an understanding is, in reality, a Action because there is working with you in connection with some matters a group called the commissioners of internal economy sometimes referred to facetiously as being the commissioners of infernal economy-yourself excluded from that facetious reference. Section 18 of the House of Commons Act provides the following:
All sums of money voted by parliament upon such estimates or payable to members of the House of Commons under the Senate and House of Commons Act, are subject to the order of the commissioners, or any three of them of whom the Speaker shall be one.
We see from this that even after parliament approves the estimates of expenditure with regard to certain matters which come under your jurisdiction, the money voted is still subject to cabinet interference and influence as to the manner in which those funds are to be expended.
As was transmitted to the house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on opening day, the commissioners of internal economy are the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Veterans Affairs who is also the leader of the house, the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I say that in effect this allows for cabinet dictatorship and cabinet control over certain functions of the House of Commons and certain activities of ours. I say this is not compatible with our sense of democracy and is not compatible with our desire to have a Speaker free and unfettered by cabinet dictation.
The background to the establishment of the commissioners of internal economy is referred to briefly in the Audit Office Guide put out by the office of the Auditor General. On page 95 of that publication for 1958, reference no. 347, the following appears:
Unlike the case in the Senate, the Speaker is elected by the House of Commons and has financial responsibilities before and after the grant of supply, because sections 16 and 18 of the House of Commons Act provide that-
Then the text goes on to recite sections 16 and 18. I shall go on to quote the reference in the Audit Office Guide, which reads as follows:
By way of explanation of the origin of the requirement in section 16 that the commissioners be members of the privy council: At the time of confederation sessions were relatively short and transportation facilities restricted, therefore it was felt desirable that the members of the board of internal economy should live close to Ottawa. A risk was that this might place the members of parliament in the Ottawa area in a preferred position; moreover, they had a special interest in appointments. The solution was to select ministers of departments who represented different parts of Canada but necessarily spent most of their time in Ottawa.
The indication, therefore, is that this board or group of commissioners came into being to meet a particular set of circumstances prevailing at that time in order to provide for the more expeditious despatch of this sort of business. I submit that those circumstances no longer exist and that we should move away from a situation where the internal affairs of this house are being run by a minister of the crown, usually the Minister of Finance, to a situation where the house has control of its own activities.
The bill in this regard seeks, therefore, to repeal section 16 of the House of Commons Act which provides-I shall not read it in detail-that the governor in council shall appoint four privy councillors who, along with yourself, Mr. Speaker, would be members of a commission for certain purposes. The bill before us also provides for the repeal of section 18 which sets up these commissioners who may approve or disapprove of the expenditure of certain sums of money. By repealing these two sections we leave the way open for the House of Commons, without interference either from the Senate or from His Excellency the Governor General, to establish standing orders to deal with this matter, because it is purely a matter with which we as members are concerned.
I think that in our consideration of what standing orders should apply to such a commission as the one over which you now preside-and I still think that one should exist- we should take into account the necessity of having, certainly, yourself as a member of that commission. It should be representative of all the parties which might happen to be in the house and, as well, of the government itself as an element distinct from parties. Naturally, I think that Mr. Speaker should, without question, continue to be chairman of this commission and that the others would work with him and advise him on certain matters. I think the Leader of the Opposition, by virtue of his office, or his deputy, should be a member of the commission also, as well as the house leaders of other parties which may be represented from time to time in the house. I think the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary secretary should likewise be

a member of the commission because there is a certain financial interest here involving the preparation of estimates. I think the Minister of Public Works or his parliamentary secretary should be a member of this board because there are certain activities affecting the area around the House of Commons and in the house itself which come under the jurisdiction of that minister. In addition, I think there should be a number of other members, perhaps five or six, who would be selected on the basis of their experience in the house.
This commission, which would be established by our standing orders and thus become directly an arm of the house itself should, I think, be set up afresh with each parliament and continue in effect for the duration of that particular parliament. I think the commission could continue to perform some of the functions carried out by the present commissioners of internal economy with respect to staff and so on. Certainly it would advise Mr. Speaker on such questions as the preparation of the estimates, the location of accommodation, office supplies and the like, including the provision of office equipment and secretarial services to members-all those things which may be considered necessary to allow a member of parliament to discharge his functions and responsibilities in the most effective manner.

It is a question of making sure that the expenditure of the money is not subject to interference and that the operation of the house comes under the control of the Speaker. Once parliament authorizes expenditures for salaries of employees of the public service those funds are paid to civil servants on a 26207-1-981

monthly basis. There is no question of derogation of responsibility. It remains the responsibility of parliament to pass on the expenditures. It is merely a question of taking into account all the factors that should be considered in preparing estimates for the coming year. The house will be the main element concerned. Each department prepares its estimates and pares them down to the bare minimum expected to be spent in the coming year.
The commission should continue to make an annual report to parliament concerning what is going on. Wages, hours and working conditions should be reported on to ensure that the staff of the House of Commons does not suffer through being underpaid or not having a channel through which to air their grievances.
I hope that no one will interpret my remarks as being disrespectful of Mr. Speaker or Your Honour's office. This merely represents an attempt to bring these provisions relating to the operation of the house up to date to ensure that Mr. Speaker will remain free and unfettered from cabinet dictation, as I said earlier, with respect to the operation of the house, this chamber and the buildings. I seek to assure that the operation will be within the control of parliament and not something the cabinet runs to suit itself.
I will close by quoting from a reprint of an article by Professor J. R. Mallory of McGill University which appeared in the February 1, 1957 issue of the Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science. Professor Mallory writes:
Cabinet government and the modern party system have placed the executive in a position of effective mastery over the House of Commons. When it is pushed to its extreme limits the ascendency of the cabinet goes somewhat against the grain of the constitution, so that certain transparent fictions must be solemnly perpetuated in constitutional doctrine. One of these is the doctrine that the House of Commons is master of its own procedure- a notion which in practice does not disturb the peace of mind of the government or its party whips. Another polite and harmless fiction surrounds the appropriation of funds for the internal administration of the House of Commons.
I am eager to ensure that there is a lessening of cabinet control over certain of the activities of the House of Commons.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the hon. member who introduced this bill is under a misapprehension with regard to the operation and function of the committee on internal economy. Throughout the course of his remarks he iterated and reiterated that there was cabinet interference, cabinet domination and cabinet control of this committee. Actually, the members of the committee act as

Private Bills
an advisory council to Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker in due course reports to parliament as to the action taken by the committee on internal economy during the course of the year. That report is subject to scrutiny by the House of Commons and is subject to debate thereon. Questions may be asked of Mr. Speaker with regard to the activities of the committee during the course of the consideration of the estimates of Mr. Speaker when they are before the House of Commons, so that there is nothing concealed with regard to the activities of the committee. Energetic and active members of the House of Commons who wish to do so can read the reports of that committee and question Mr. Speaker when his estimates are before the house. There is no cabinet domination or interference with the activities of Mr. Speaker in this regard.
The hon. member suggests we should bring the situation up to date. Actually what he is suggesting is that we turn back the clock approximately 95 years because it was in 1878 that the committee on internal economy, as we know it, was set up. It succeeded an earlier committee which was called the committee on contingencies. That committee which normally consisted of 21 members functioned during the time when the legislative assemblies were active in the governmental life of our country prior to confederation. The committee was appointed after confederation and dealt with problems concerning the House of Commons. In 1868 the prime minister of the day, Sir John A. Macdonald, introduced a bill based on British precedents to establish the committee on internal economy. It has functioned from that day to this without, to my knowledge, any suggestion that it has not been a competent and responsible body, responsible to the House of Commons.
I am at a loss to know why the hon. member has seized upon this opportunity of bringing to the house this particular aspect of the statutes. I do not know whether or not the hon. member was inspired to do so simply on the basis of a magazine article by Professor Mallory. The portion the hon. gentleman quoted seemed to me not to be conclusive evidence that a change should be made. In fact, as I followed his discourse I could not find any argument in favour of change except the unfounded allegation as indicated in some of the words he used that there is undue cabinet influence and interference with the spending of the money voted.
The hon. gentleman said he wished to make Mr. Speaker free and unfettered from cabinet dictation. This, too is an unfounded allegation. There is no evidence to support a statement of that nature. If it were true it would

logically follow that every speaker from 1878 to the present day has been unfree and fettered by cabinet dictation. It is a rather strange thing that in 1962 the hon. member for Skeena whose experience in the House of Commons is relatively limited should fancy that he suddenly discovers that something has been wrong for well over eighty years. The hon. gentleman is now riding off in all directions in an attempt to correct something which he thinks is wrong. I think he should examine the history of this committee, lay the facts before the house and support his allegations with evidence before he comes here to give information which is, to say the least, a bit misleading, and to launch an accusation against members of the government who happen to be on the committee on internal economy, charging them with undue influence with regard to the Speaker. As a matter of fact, I thought the hon. member was quite out of order in making accusations of that sort with regard to members of the house who are on that committee. However, I did not rise on a point of order as I realized that I would have an opportunity to speak, as has happened.
If the hon. member would look back at the Journals of 1867-68, he will find that a committee was appointed in that year. As I have said, there were 21 members. I have not had time to check and ascertain whether they were representative of all parties in the house. However, perhaps they may have been of that character.
The hon. member throws out the suggestion that all parties of the house should be represented on this committee to advise the Speaker and that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) or his deputy-I do not know whether he has a deputy now unless it is the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue)-should be a member of that committee; and for some reason or another he would be prepared to give the Leader of the Opposition a prominent position there. Then he suggests that house leaders of other parties represented here in the House of Commons should be on that committee. For what purpose? Every member who has some difficulty or complaint with regard to the internal management of the House of Commons is perfectly free to go to Mr. Speaker and to suggest to him that some changes should be made. I am quite certain that over the years that has been the practice of the House of Commons. I well remember that when I was sitting in the opposition I often called upon the Speaker of that day in order to suggest certain changes in the general operation of the House of Commons, with regard to the matter of supplies and things of that nature. At the present time there is

no particular reason to judge that the same opportunity is not available to every member of the present House of Commons with the present Speaker. Alternatively, members could draw to the attention of the named members of the committee on internal economy suggestions, if they have them, for improvements in management.
I have not had time in which to discover why, in 1878, the prime minister of the day thought it wise to change from the method of a large committee to a statutory body, namely the committee on internal economy. The librarians have been working hard to find that information but it has not yet come to light. However, there must have been some good reason for making the shift. It may be because of the financial obligation that is imposed on the Speaker. In Bourinot, the fourth edition, at page 197, I notice that the learned author of that work states the following:
The commissioners of internal economy of the House of Commons is a statutory body having definite powers and responsibilities with reference to the expenditures of that body. Formerly, certain expenses of the legislative assembly of Canada were regulated by a committee of contingencies. appointed at the opening of each session. On its report the salaries and other contingent expenses were provided for. The committee was re-appointed in 1867-8, and made several reports, which were acted upon, but during the same session, the premier (Sir John Macdonald) brought in a bill respecting the internal economy of the House of Commons, which was unanimously passed.
I draw the attention of the house to that quotation. The house of that day had lengthy experience with the committee on contingencies and members of the House of Commons of that period who had formerly served in the assemblies of Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the other provinces had similar experience. Yet when Sir John brought in his bill setting up the committee as we know it now, the house unanimously passed that measure. I therefore suggest the implication is that the house found the committee on contingencies was not a suitable method of dealing with problems affecting the members and the organization of the business of the house and thought it would be better done by having a statutory body appointed.
Mr. Bourinot on the following page goes on to indicate some of the work of that committee and he ends one of his paragraphs with this sentence:
The commissioners regulate with the Speaker all salaries not fixed by statute and all expenses of the house-in fact assist the Speaker as an advisory council with respect to the staff of the house.
Then he goes on to state that provision was made for an audit of the accounts and
Private Bills
that the Auditor General in his annual report would give the fullest information with respect to the expenditure of the two houses.
Why should we make a change at this time? If the hon. member wishes to have a change made and wishes to go back to an outdated system, I suggest that he must put forward much more valid arguments than those he has adduced this afternoon. I reject entirely the accusation that there is interference with the Speaker or that there is cabinet domination. I reject his accusation that the cabinet steps in and takes action to suit itself, again using some of his words. This is an atrocious accusation against members of the cabinet. The article which he quoted from the Audit Office Guide of 1958, gave an explanation of the Auditor General of that period as to why the commissioners were appointed by the privy council. I do not know where the Auditor General of that day obtained his information. However, it has been reprinted in the explanatory section of the bill. Apparently the suggestion made there is that instead of just appointing members who were living close to Ottawa because of transportation difficulties of 100 years ago, it would give better representation countrywide to appoint to the committee members from the cabinet who would be living in Ottawa anyway but who would be representing other parts of the country. So it was not in order to ensure or make any provision for so-called cabinet domination, but merely to make the committee widely representative of the various areas of Canada that members of the privy council were appointed to the committee. There was no plot in those days and there is none at the present time to bring about domination by members of the cabinet. In addition, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that members of the cabinet are also members of the House of Commons and should be entitled to the same consideration as other members of this august body.
It is interesting to read the report of the committee that was set up in 1867 and 1868. I judge this was the last time that the committee of contingencies operated prior to the bringing in of the bill of Sir John A. Macdonald. The House of Commons dealt with 17 resolutions which were put forward in the third report of the committee of contingencies. It is interesting to note that they were concerned with matters of financial economy to be observed in the House of Commons. They dealt with the number of translators and the number of extra clerks that should be employed. They considered such things as the reception and distribution of the printed bills and other documents. They dealt with the subject of the post office and its management. They suggested

Private Bills
that no clerk be stationed in the reading room, that there should be but two messengers and one labourer in the joint department on routine and printing, that there be but one messenger in the library and that no messenger be attached to the office of the Speaker's secretary or to that of the assistant clerk of the house.
They set the salaries of various people employed by the House of Commons. They suggested that the nine pages, which was the number they had working in those days, should receive $1.50 per day during the session. They suggested that the salaries of the two night watchmen be fixed at $400 per annum, that the stationery supplied to each member of the house should not exceed in cost the sum of $15 for each session and should be delivered in a box on the first day of each session, and that no more be issued. They were dealing with matters of internal management with regard to the House of Commons.
I suggest that those matters are being dealt with effectively and efficiently at the present time through the committee on internal economy under the able chairmanship of the Speaker with the assistance of his very able staff, and that the House of Commons has full opportunity during the course of a session to examine into the activities of that committee and to question the Speaker when his estimates are before the house with regard to how his duties have been carried out. It follows from that that there is no concealment in this committee, no pressure applied by members of the committee who happen to be members of the privy council, and that the Speaker is completely free and unfettered in the performance of his duties.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few brief remarks on this rather intriguing bill. The explanatory notes state that the purpose of the bill is to abolish statutory rule by members of

the Queen's privy council over the internal economy of this house, the reasons for such rule no longer having validity, and thus permit the Speaker and members chosen by the house to govern the affairs of the commons.
I must say before proceeding with my remarks that the minister did not deny that the purpose of the bill is properly stated in the explanatory notes. The purpose of the bill is to assist Mr. Speaker and members. It is quite obvious to one who has knowledge of the management of the internal affairs of this house that Your Honour reigns but does not govern in all respects, and the purpose of the bill is to assist Mr. Speaker to govern with the assistance of members of this house, to introduce a greater spirit of democracy, shall I say, in the administration.
I thought that the minister was rather sharp with the hon. member for Skeena. He will admit that the member has provoked discussion on a somewhat obscure and complicated question. Practically the whole of the minister's reply to the arguments of the member for Skeena was a defence of the status quo. He showed a rigidity and inflexibility of mind that is so common among persons of Tory mentality. He did not even suggest to the member for Skeena that there was something in what he had said and that the matter should be looked into because the subject warranted investigation. I think that would have been a much more progressive approach on the part of the minister. I trust that he really and finally has been influenced by the arguments of the member for Skeena and will change his mind. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, good precedents for his doing so have recently been established in the house in that the minister has been influenced by arguments put before the house by members of this group and has changed his mind. I do hope he will return to that former flexibility and give this matter further consideration.
I thought that the minister rather censured the member for Skeena somewhat unduly. This is a most complicated and obscure question and the member for Skeena demonstrated absolutely his fitness to be placed in the shadow cabinet which we hope to form in the very near future. On page 32 of the publication, Organization of the Government of Canada, I read the following:
In the House of Commons, when the language of the Speaker is English, the language of the chairman of committees, who also acts as Deputy Speaker, is French. In addition to presiding at aE meetings of the house, the Speaker enforces the observance of its rules, maintains its rights and privileges and acts as the official spokesman of the house as occasion may require.

I might say, Mr. Speaker, that you do that to the great satisfaction of all of us.
He is also responsible to the house for the management of its internal affairs and the operation of its branches and services.
That is not quite an accurate description of the circumstances that prevail at the present time with respect to Mr. Speaker, and the purpose of the bill is to make that statement a matter of fact so far as the management of the affairs of the house is concerned. I must compliment the member for Skeena on his exposition of a somewhat abstruse and to the public, I am sure, mysterious administrative problem concerning the management of the affairs of this house. It is not a subject that would be easily understood outside the house and I think there is too little knowledge among members within the house. Although there has been a very unsympathetic approach on the part of members of the government party, I trust that this discussion will cause members to do some reading and find out the exact circumstances that prevail at the .present time.
However, he has provided an opportunity for members to discuss the improvement of what I consider, in some respects, to be our out of date way of doing things, our out of date system of internal management. What the hon. member is aiming to do is to improve the management of this house so that there will be greater satisfaction amongst members with respect to offices, secretaries and things of that sort. Mr. Speaker does the very best he can for us under the present circumstances, but there is a sort of limiting hand behind the scenes when it comes to finances, staff and so on. This method would improve the control of expenditures and the application of those expenditures. It would improve the circumstances of the staff and give them a sense of security to which they are entitled and which does not prevail at the present time because of this hidden hand behind the scenes. I am not suggesting for a moment that these gentlemen do not perform their duties to the best of their ability, but under present circumstances we have a variety of pre-Victorian management which is out of date.
I am sure that even the discussion of this problem will inform members, and the passage of this bill provide greater satisfaction to members in the performance of their duties, establish fair rules for the staff and introduce improvements and efficiency in the management of the internal affairs of the House of Commons. In saying that, I am not reflecting upon any person. The hon. member for Skeena is seeking to improve a system which we believe, in some respects, has become somewhat outdated.

speechtext: I should like to make a few remarks in connection with this amendment to the Farm Improvement Loans Act based

on some of the experience I have had in assisting farmers in my area to obtain loans under this measure.
I am very much in agreement with those who have spoken about the importance of this measure. Indeed, it is becoming difficult for those engaged in agriculture to obtain credit, when they need it, from any other source. I do know of some people in my own area who have attempted unsuccessfully to obtain assistance. Finally, they had to borrow from individuals at the rate of 10 per cent plus a bonus before they could get a loan. There is no doubt that the act has been very helpful to a great many people.
However, I have some reservations about increasing the amount available for these loans from time to time. I think that at some point we must take a realistic look at where we are heading. I noticed in tonight's Citizen an article suggesting that there might be two new provinces in northern Canada and that the possibilities for agriculture in those areas were terrific. It seems we have a lot of people who are doing research directed towards increasing production without a corresponding effort being made to find markets to dispose of the products we have on hand at the present time. I think this aspect is important.
I do know it has been the policy of the farm loans board to suggest for example, that a certain farmer with, say, 20 dairy cows should have 35 cows. To my mind that is not the right approach, because we are encouraging farmers to increase dairy production at a time when we are faced with a surplus of dairy products. Again, we should not encourage western farmers to buy more machinery so as to produce more wheat when we do not have a market for all the wheat we are producing at the present time. The same remarks apply to producers of sugar beets and to a great many others. It seems to me there should be some way of controlling the amount of loans going to those who are producing today just about what the market demands. In my experience it is not hard for a farmer, especially if he is doing well, to go to a bank and receive favourable consideration of an application for a loan under this measure. On the other hand, a small farmer, or a farmer who is really pressed and in need of assistance, would find it difficult to get such a loan through a bank.
There is another aspect which concerns me. I believe that when a farmer applies for a loan to buy cattle the bankers interpret the loan as being made in respect of purebred cattle. I know of one person in my area who paid between $450 and $500 apiece for cows, though he was selling his milk to a manufacturing plant. It seems to me that purebred herds may have their advantages but
Farm Improvement Loans Act that we are certainly placing many of these farmers in a position where they are going to find it difficult to repay their loans. These people would be in a better position, it seems to me, if they were allowed to buy good quality dairy cattle and were not confined to purebred stock. I have talked with three bankers in my town in connection with this situation and they tell me that this practice is followed for the purpose of identifying the cattle; were it not for the registration number they would have no way of identifying these cattle. That seems ridiculous to me, because when they make a loan they know how many cows that farmer should have, and the farmer is bound to maintain his herd at a certain level.
Although I am in favour of seeing these loans increased, I think there should be some changes made in the regulations so that a farmer should not be able to borrow to increase his herd or buy more machinery merely to produce something which is already in surplus. I feel this is what is happening in some cases under the provisions of the act. It seems to me that our officials, when approving loans, should be encouraging farmers to get into lines which are not already overproduced-something that they can market. I am afraid that if we continue the present policy we shall find ourselves in the future in a more difficult position than we are at the present time.

I thank hon. members for the support they have expressed for this resolution. I shall try to deal with several points which were raised by hon. members who sought information.
First of all, one hon. member asked why the act is being extended for a three year period. That has been the history of this legislation since it was introduced in 1945. As I understand it the purpose has been to retain parliamentary control so that parliament would have the opportunity of reviewing the legislation once every three years.
There is a substantial amount of money placed by way of guarantee at the disposal of this legislation. The view has commended itself to parliament that on this account as well as for other reasons that form of control should be retained in the form of a limited life to the legislation.
Second, I was asked by the hon. member for Gloucester in regard to the position of credit unions and caisses populaires. We had an extended debate on this subject in 1960 and there has been no change in the position since that time.
Reference was made to the limit on the individual loan. May I remind hon. members that the original amount of an individual loan under this legislation was $3,000. That

Farm Improvement Loans Act was increased to $4,000 in 1953, to $5,000 in 1956 and to $7,500 in 1959. That last increase was, of course, the largest increase to date. It was an increase of 50 per cent in the previous total and I think under present conditions it can be regarded as reasonably adequate. Conditions, of course, could change and one recognizes that both with respect to equipment and to other investment in agriculture, today the stress is on an increase in investment.
The hon. member for Assiniboia asked me for certain information of a statistical nature in relation to the experience with repossession of machinery. I shall make inquiries in that regard. I cannot say that that information could be made available before this legislation has passed through its various stages. I can tell the hon. member, however, that the administration of this legislation so far as the Department of Finance is concerned has been thorough and systematic as well as sympathetic.
In the calendar year 1961 the total of loans made was 70,615. The number of claims made in respect of the guarantee given under the legislation was only 232. In the calendar year 1960 the number of loans was 68,041 and the number of claims was only 209, so the experience of administration of this legislation is in keeping with what I said last night concerning the record of losses. It is an enviable record. I think it points to the sound policies that have been followed in relation to lending under this act as well as to the sturdy reliability of the Canadian farmer.
Finally, the hon. member for Welland asked me about the position of fire insurance on farm equipment. It is quite obvious to hon. members that no bank manager is going to make a loan on farm machinery unless he has reasonable fire insurance on the particular equipment. The hon. member said he knew of several cases where there had been loss by fire and where evidently there had not been insurance. In that case I must express my surprise. I can only surmise that there has been some slip up on the part of the bank or on the part of the borrower in that case. Perhaps there was fire insurance on the equipment at the time the loan was placed. It may have lapsed later or for some reason or other may have become invalid. It would be sheer speculation or surmise to attempt to account for it. Sound banking practice will dictate on the part of the bank


manager firm insistence on having fire insurance placed on equipment which is the subject of a loan under this legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution, as I am sure hon. members are aware, is a kindred resolution to the one which has just been passed. This one relates to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act as the former one did to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The purpose of the proposed amendment is to extend operations under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act for a further period of three years by establishing a new lending period to run from July 1, 1962 to June 30, 1965.
This legislation offers to fishermen credit facilities similar to those provided under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Thus, it will be sufficient, I think, to recall at this time some of the main features of the act. The essential purpose of the legislation is to facilitate the provision of term loans to fishermen. To this end, credit is made available to finance a broad range of investment projects including the purchase, construction or improvement of fishing vessels, fishing equipment and shore installations. The maximum amount that may be borrowed by a fisherman is $4,000 and repayment of the loan may take place over a period as long as eight years. Under the provisions of the act, the government undertakes to reimburse individual lending institutions for losses of up to 15 per cent of loans aggregating $500,000. A guarantee of

10 per cent is applicable in respect to loan funds exceeding $500,000. There is an over-all limit on the total amount of guaranteed loans which may be made by all lending institutions and this has been set at $20 million.
This legislation was enacted by parliament in 1955 and was made effective for a period of three years. In 1959, an amendment was passed which extended the period during which guaranteed loans might be made from December 12, 1958, to June 30, 1962. The amendment which is now proposed will establish the third lending period since the inception of the act. In this brief review of the history of the legislation, I might also point out that another amendment was enacted in 1959 which extended the definition of a fisherman to include a person who intends to acquire an interest in a fishing vessel, as well as a person who already has an interest in one.
In recent years a fairly stable although modest amount of lending has taken place under this legislation.
From the inception of the act in 1955 to December, 1961, a total of 981 loans was made amounting to $1,237,328. Of this total, $813,717 was repaid and currently an amount of $423,611 is outstanding. The most recent annual report on operations under the act shows that during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1961, an amount slightly in excess of $217,000 was lent to fishermen, comprising 142 individual loans. During the succeeding nine month period to December 31, 1961, a total of 127 loans was made amounting to $187,454.
In summary, the proposed amendment is simple and brief. It will extend the period during which guaranteed loans may be made and, as a result, fishermen will continue to have available intermediate term credit facilities for borrowing, on reasonable terms and conditions, to meet their capital needs. I believe that this measure, together with other action taken by the government, will enable fishermen to take advantage of more efficient methods of operation and will help to ensure the sound development of this important primary industry.

This is a rather low cost type of boat, so far as the west coast is concerned. I do not care to engage in any guesswork about the cost of fishing vessels on the east coast. I leave that to those who are more familiar with that area. In so far as the west coast is concerned, $4,000 would not buy a rowboat that could be used for fishing. The act now prohibits a person who does not own a fishing vessel from borrowing money. We know there are many commercial fishermen who, for one reason or another, will remove themselves from the fishing industry for a period of a year or two or perhaps more. If they have an interest in a boat, they sell it. If they own a boat, they sell the boat and take up some other form of work. Perhaps two or three years later they may decide to enter the industry again. They are definitely prohibited from borrowing under this act because they do not have an interest in any vessel. This is one type of amendment that should be made in order to help people who want to borrow money to get back into the fishing industry. However, as I have said, you cannot borrow money unless you have an interest in a fishing vessel.
In any event, in the final analysis it is the lending agency that decides whether or not to lend money to these individuals. It is not the Minister of Finance. He is not lending money to anybody. He gets the hull completed on the ways, but he cannot borrow money under this legislation to enable him to complete that boat by reason of the fact that he is not considered to be one who has an interest in a fishing vessel. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, when I am suggesting an increase in the limit of $4,000 on loans to $8,000 or $10,000, I am treading on dangerous ground because the section of the act which contains this provision is the same section which provides for 5 per cent simple interest on the loans. Perhaps if the minister could get into that field he would treat the fishermen with the same contempt he treated the small businessmen by having a wide open interest rate inserted in this legislation. As I have said, we went through this procedure once before. Like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I feel that this is a piece of legislation which, inadequate though it is, the house could put through with a minimum amount of controversy. Certainly, so far as I am concerned, that could be done. The resolution which is before us for discussion now has to do with nothing more than a minor amendment to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act to extend to June 30, 1965 the period during which guaranteed loans may be made. In introducing this resolution, the minister said this act was similar to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. As stated by my colleague, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act contains a definition of "lender" which includes credit unions, caisses populaires and other co-operative credit societies designated by the minister as lenders for the purpose of the act. I would say this is the major difference between this act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act which we discussed this afternoon.
Now, the minister has put on the record some of the figures relating to the application of this act. When we realize that the amount authorized for lending under this act is limited to $20 million and the act has been used only to the extent of $1,200,000 by 614 fishermen in a period of six years, we can state that it has certainly been used in a very modest way. At the moment the
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act amount outstanding under loans made under this act is in the vicinity of $600,000. As was stated by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, out of the total number of loans made, 474 or about 50 per cent have been repaid for a total of $660,000, and there were no claims paid during the year. One claim amounting to $237.64 has been paid. This clearly shows that the fishermen are meeting their obligations.
In 1959, when an amendment to this act was introduced, representations were made to the minister to the effect that there was not enough publicity given to the act, not enough fishermen knew the act existed, and there was a definite reluctance on the part of the chartered banks to make loans under this act.
I think that some major amendment should be effected to make this act more practical and more adaptable to the needs of the fishermen. The act should be amended to assist fishermen in the case of disaster. If a fisherman, for example, loses his boat and fishing gear he is in no position to make the down payment which is required by the chartered banks. If the act were amended so that the amount guaranteed by the government were 25 per cent instead of 15 per cent in the case of a major loss by a fisherman, I am convinced that more fishermen would take advantage of this measure.
I would therefore suggest that before the bill is introduced the minister gives further consideration to it and includes in it some major amendment which will be of some assistance to fishermen.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add my voice to hon. members who have already spoken urging the minister to give consideration to extending the scope of this legislation. As the minister told us, this legislation was set up in 1955 to fill a specific need. Now, after more than five years experience with it, we know it is not doing the job it was intended to do and is not coming anywhere near filling the need that has to be met.
The minister told us that the amount lent under this act has been very modest. In a parliamentary return that was tabled in this house some time ago it was shown that since the inception of this legislation only 854 loans have been made from December, 1955 right up till the end of March, 1961. That has worked out to less than $200,000 per year.
In my own province of Newfoundland, during that time only 10 loans have been made, one in 1955-56 for $750; two in 1956-57 for $1,000 in total; in 1957-58 and 1958-59 there were no loans at all; in 1959-60 there were two loans totalling $2,448, and in 1960-61
15S0

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act there were five loans totalling $8,065. Altogether in the entire period from December 12, 1955 right up to the end of March, 1961 only 10 loans were made, for an aggregate of $11,753.
The minister told us when he introduced this legislation that its purpose was to enable fishermen to acquire vessels, to acquire shares in fishing vessels and to modernize their equipment. How many vessels can you buy for $11,000, or for an average of $2,000 per year; how much equipment can you get?
This is vital to our province because the fishing industry is one of the mainstays of our economy. We have about 18,000 fishermen making a livelihood out of the fishery, and the fishery is one of the industries that is self-perpetuating and is certainly capable of being expanded and modernized to compete with the fisheries of other countries.
The fisherman is a small operator, for the most part, and he needs more assistance than he can get under this legislation. The hon. member for Skeena has pointed out some of the difficulties, and I am not going to repeat what I have said on so many occasions in this house, that it is impossible for the ordinary fisherman in my province to get loans from the banks. I think that is amply proven by the fact that in six years only 10 loans totalling under $12,000 were made. For a vital industry of a country, this kind of lending cannot have any impact at all. There is just as much need-I would say, an even far greater need-on the part of fishermen as there is on the part of farmers. This legislation is not meeting the need that has to be met, and that must be met if we are going to modernize our industry and put it on a sound economic basis. For these reasons I should like to add my voice to those of hon. members who have already urged the minister to either change this legislation or set up some other means of filling this need.
