Mr. Chairman, the resolution before us is:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act to extend the period during which guaranteed loans may be made to the 30th day of June, 1965.
Obviously if this act is going to be used at all, the payment period would have to be extended, but after all it is a very minor amendment to a piece of legislation which I would have hoped would have been a greater advantage to the fishermen and would have been used more readily.
I think the experience we have had with this act over the last few years shows that it has not had the appeal to fishermen that we all wished it would have. I think one
of the things that should be done in amending this act is to make a study to determine why the act has not done for the fishermen what it was intended to do, and why it has not received the attention and use by the fishermen that we would normally expect. I think an effort should be made to find out why.
There can be no doubt about the need as far as my province is concerned. There are three or four areas in my constituency where, if men are going to make a living, they have to resort to the fishing industry. They now do not have the boats, they do not have the gear, they do not have the inshore fishing property that would allow them to make a living which is compatible with our cost of living today. Perhaps years ago, under the conditions which existed at that time they were able to make a living of sorts. Today their needs are greater, and if they are going to make a living out of the fishing industry they must be able to fish earlier in the year. They must be able to carry on their fishing activities later in the year, and all this demands bigger, stronger and better equipment. If these men are going to need bigger, stronger and better equipment, as they do, it means a larger investment, and the only way in which these people can get funds to improve their equipment is by getting loans. Our Newfoundland fishermen for some reason or other are finding it difficult to get loans under this act. As my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo has just stated, very few loans have been made to Newfoundland fishermen under this measure. I feel there is some reason for this, and an investigation into those reasons would be very worth while in order that the act might be amended in such a way as to give our fishermen the loans they need to continue to make a living in the industry.

It may surprise some hon. members who have spoken on the subject to learn that experience has shown that there has been no crowding of that ceiling. My examination of the record indicates that the fishermen of British Columbia have taken greater advantage of the act than those in other provinces not with respect to the number of applications but with respect to the total value of the loans, which indicates that loans on the west coast are higher in value than those in the maritimes. Some fishermen who have knowledge of this act, knowing they can borrow money, make inquiries and discover the amount they can borrow is limited to $4,000. Knowing that, even though they may need $8,000 or $9,000 they realize they would be wasting their time trying to get that much from the bank. They therefore arrange their finances in such a way as to permit them to operate within the loan they will receive or try to curtail expenses and skimp on what they could do if they received a larger loan.

I should like to take a moment to express my views with regard to this piece of legislation now before the committee. Coming as I do from a riding in which there are a great number of shore fishermen, it has been my experience that this act has been of very little use to the people to whom it was intended to be of assistance. The shore fishermen are by far the greatest proportion of people engaged in the fishery in the Atlantic provinces, though it is quite true that the largest proportion of the catch is landed by people fishing from larger boats and operating out of the modern processing plants. Some
15,000	families are dependant directly upon the shore fishery in the province of Nova Scotia.
These are the people who need some special new type of credit facilities. They have found the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act to be of very little use to them for the simple reason that the bankers for some reason or other will not extend sufficient credit under the act. Since the act provides a guarantee of 15 per cent of a portion of any loans made under it and ten per cent of the balance, one would think that this type of loan was one which would recommend itself to the banks. However, it has been my experience and that of a great many of my constituents who have got in touch with me from time to time with regard to this matter that the act is of very little use in practical effect. I wonder whether the minister would make some inquiry to ascertain whether there is not some way in which the act could be of more use to the shore fishermen for whom it was designed. It may be that this is only a matter of bringing to the attention of the banking community that this act could be of great benefit to the shore fishermen if it were applied with more flexibility.
I notice that in 1961 very few loans were approved in the province of Nova Scotia. I suppose that next to Newfoundland, it is the province which has the largest number of

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act shore fishermen in Canada. In 1961 in Nova Scotia, only some $21,691 of loans were approved, yet the record of loans made under this act so far has been that these loans were repaid. The department has suffered little loss, I understand, in claims made under this legislation. It is too bad that some way could not be found to make more credit available to the shore fishermen. I am sure that some other method is needed rather than this particular type of legislation. My colleague from Westmorland a few minutes ago mentioned that he thought the best idea would be to set up a credit corporation for fishermen similar to that used for farm credit. I think this would be a very good idea. It may well be that this whole problem of credit for the shore fishermen and the rural dweller in general should be examined by a royal commission or some other type of inquiry. I am sure no other section of this nation is more in need of rejuvenation or rehabilitation than are the people engaged in the shore fishery. There are some fishing districts in the province of Nova Scotia-and I am sure this is so in the other provinces in the Atlantic area as well-who are as much in need of redevelopment as are some areas receiving aid under the Colombo plan.
I should like to see an inquiry made towards setting up some sort of credit system which would encompass the wider needs of the people in rural areas, particularly in the maritime section. I find that it is impossible really to say that very many fishermen subsist by their shore fishery alone. Shore fishermen usually are part time fishermen, part time lumbermen and part time farmers. Yet there is no one agency to which this group of people can go to seek over-all credit. They either must qualify as full time fishermen as under this act, or as full time farmers under other legislation. I should like to see some sort of rural assistance program set up which would allow a man who is receiving part of his income from the fishery, part from farming and part from lumbering, to go to one source where he would get adequate credit to help him to carry on his entire business operation, which requires him to look to the fruits of the sea, of the land and of the forests at once. The problems of the people in rural areas, particularly along our sea coast who rely chiefly upon the fishing industry for their livelihood and who turn in other seasons to other parts of the economy, needs special attention now, ahead of any other sector of the Canadian community.
I would sincerely recommend to the Minister of Finance, whom we have found to take our suggestions very readily in matters of this kind, that he see whether there is some way in which an adequate system of

credit for the shore fishing industry could be set up. I can tell him that it would be a great boon to a section of the population which badly needs some help in this sector.

Mr. Chairman, we can all
appreciate that conditions in the fishing industry on the east coast require at least some extra degree of consideration with respect to action by this government or any government for that matter. Earlier this session we spent a considerable amount of time discussing the question of subsidies or payments or whatever they are called to western grain producers on the basis of $1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of $200 for some nebulous purpose. I believe that over three years the total amount payable on the basis of $1 per acre exceeds some $120 million. I do not know whether the Minister of Finance is agreeable to paying $1 per cubic mile of fished ocean up to a certain maximum to assist the fishermen to get by in the world, but this situation is one that we should attempt to bring into

some balance. If it is equitable and correct to pay western grain growers as primary producers of food a subsidy on an acreage basis, surely in order to bring about some balance with respect to government assistance to primary producers of other foodstuffs, and especially in view of the deteriorating condition of the fishing industry on the west coast as well as on the east coast, we should be considering some means of payment to fishermen in order to bring their incomes into balance and afford them a better opportunity to participate in the economic life of the country.
As I say, I do not know whether it would operate on the basis of $1 per cubic mile of ocean fished, on the basis of so many cents per mile for the mileage that fishing vessels travel to and from port or whether a subsidy would be paid at least to the fishermen on the east coast who have to fish outside the 12 mile limit whereas foreign vessels can fish inside the limit. I do not know what the basis would be but the government should be searching for some plan.
The proposal of so much per cubic mile of ocean fished may sound like an idea taken from outer space, but surely it is within the realm of the imagination of the government to accept the idea and develop it, particularly in view of the fact that there is going to be an election shortly.

Mr. Chairman, the measure referred to in the resolution is another step in the efforts of the federal government to strengthen the fiscal position of the provinces and through them to aid the municipalities also. It will subject 28 named federal crown corporations to the payment of provincial sales taxes, gasoline taxes and automobile and truck licences, waiving their constitutional immunity from such taxes. It will achieve approximate equality of treatment as between provincial crown corporations and agencies in relation to federal sales and excise taxes, on the one hand, and federal crown corporations and agencies in relation to provincial retail sales taxes and gasoline taxes, on the other.
The bill will implement one of the Prime Minister's proposals to the federal-provincial conference of February 23-24, 1961. At that time the Prime Minister stated:
We have given further thought to the means of achieving reciprocity of treatment in the position of provincial crown corporations and agencies under federal sales and excise taxes and the position of federal corporations and agencies under provincial direct taxes on purchases. We are prepared to waive federal immunity from taxation and instruct federal corporations and agencies to pay provincial purchase taxes and other similar taxes on the understanding that provincial corporations and agencies will be subject to federal sales and excise taxes. We think that this is an equitable arrangement, being in accordance with the general principles followed in regard to the payment of federal taxes on purchases by federal departments. We think it is better than reciprocal exemptions as an administrative and accounting arrangement, preserving as it will a fairer relationship between crown corporations and agencies in general and private businesses.
The federal government now enjoys a constitutional advantage over the provinces in the imposition of taxes because of its exclusive right to impose indirect taxes. Neither level of government has power to tax the other directly. The provinces have no power to impose indirect taxes. The federal government, having such powers, could collect sales and excise taxes from manufacturers and wholesalers selling to the provinces and the manufacturers and wholesalers could pass the tax along to the provincial governments in

Crown Corporations
the form of increased prices although there would be no actual levy of tax on the crown in the right of the province. The provincial governments, on the other hand, lacking the power to impose indirect taxes, cannot so easily impose taxes which are passed on to the federal government, although undoubtedly certain provincial direct taxes become elements of cost and are in this way passed on to the federal government.
In actual fact, the federal government has never pressed its constitutional advantage to the limit and has voluntarily provided a statutory exemption in respect of goods purchased for use by provincial departments, with the result that its sales and excise taxes impinge upon the provinces only through their crown corporations and agencies.
It is therefore apparent that the federal government, by instructing its own corporations and agencies to pay provincial sales taxes, is making a unilateral concession which will have the approximate effect of placing the two levels of government on the same footing. I have stated only that approximate equality of treatment would be achieved by the proposed bill. It is, frankly, difficult to make a more precise claim because of the real problem, at both the federal and provincial levels, of distinguishing between departments and agencies. Lest any hon. member should under-estimate the importance of this concession, however, may I call the attention of the committee to the fact that the bill actually goes the extra mile by providing that federal corporations shall expose themselves not only to retail sales and gasoline taxes, but also to automobile and truck licences. The latter, of course, are a provincial tax with no federal counterpart so that federal corporations will actually be exposed to provincial taxes of a greater variety than the federal taxes to which provincial agencies are now exposed.
The 28 federal crown corporations which will be instructed to pay retail sales taxes, gasoline taxes, and automobile or truck licences imposed by the provinces, are listed in the schedule to the bill. These corporations were selected after a careful scrutiny of all branches of the federal government. Essentially, they consist of all but three of the crown corporations listed under the Financial Administration Act plus those unlisted corporations which seemed comparable in function or legal status.
Concerning the corporations listed in the Financial Administration Act, these come entirely from schedules C and D since the bodies listed in schedules A and B are defined, by section 2(f) of the act, to be departments. Three corporations listed in schedule C of the act have been excluded on grounds

of principle. These agencies, Canadian Arsenals Limited, Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, and Defence Construction (1951) Limited, differ from the other schedule C and D corporations in that they operate almost entirely to provide what might be described as internal services for federal government departments. The corporations outside of the Financial Administration Act which will be covered by this bill are the Bank of Canada, Canada council, Canadian wheat board, industrial development bank, national productivity council, and the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation.
No recent estimate has been made of the cost to the 28 crown corporations of complying with the provisions of this bill. However, on the basis of a survey made in respect of the 1958 taxation year, it is estimated that the approximate cost will be $3 million. The cost would be substantially greater except for the fact that many of the crown corporations listed in the schedule are already voluntarily paying all or some of the taxes with which this bill is concerned. The effect of the bill, therefore, will be to place all 28 corporations on the same footing concerning the payment of sales taxes, gasoline taxes, and automobile or truck licences.
These are the main features of the proposed legislation. It represents an important concession to the provinces and marks the first time in history that this federal immunity has been waived for their benefit. It will accordingly contribute to the fiscal strength and independence of the provinces.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CERTAIN PROVINCIAL TAXES AND FEES
speechtext:
We have before us a very interesting resolution which will be followed by a bill that we will read with great interest. As I recall the circumstances in perhaps the largest province of Canada, Ontario, which had a government favourable to the present government in so far as its political inclinations were concerned, the government of that province went on strike. The government of Premier Frost decided that it did not intend to permit its crown entities to pay sales taxes to the federal government. The government of Ontario felt that there was a difficulty here and stopped, as I say, paying these taxes.
The Minister of Finance indicates that the federal government has decided, out of great generosity, to pay something that it was not being pressed to pay. I want to say that if the Prime Minister, on the basis of reciprocity told an interprovincial conference in February, 1961, that he was prepared to do something along this line, he was just 12 months behind the times. I think the reason he is doing something is that the province of Ontario, a relatively friendly government to the present federal government, stopped

paying sales taxes to the federal government in respect of the purchases of such big provincial crown corporations as Ontario hydro.
Before proceeding too much further, I think we should hear from the Minister of Finance as to whether or not he has been receiving sales taxes levied by the federal government from Ontario crown corporations. I should like to know how long there has been a default in the payment of sales taxes with respect to Ontario hydro. I should like to know if there is no default at the moment, whether there was, in fact, a default a year ago and for how long that default existed. How many millions of dollars were involved in the payments withheld by Ontario hydro and other provincial crown corporations? It is all very well for the Minister of Finance to suggest that this is something that was proffered to the provincial government. I say it was not. This government resisted and complained about the fact that the province of Ontario felt it should not pay sales taxes to the federal government.
Now, the federal government, through its crown corporations such as Polymer and many others with almost similar commercial operations, refuse to pay the Ontario tax on gasoline purchases or the normal licence fees for vehicles operated by the corporation within the province. I say that we had an impasse between two Conservative governments, the government at Queen's Park and the government at Ottawa. There may be other provinces in which similar difficulties have been experienced. I expect that during this debate we will hear from British Columbia members as to what their feelings are with respect to this proposal, particularly in so far as the purchase of the British Columbia Electric Company is concerned, which until recently was not a provincial entity. I hope we will hear more about that.
I want to say that the Minister of Finance has gone far out of line in suggesting that this is an act of generosity on the part of the federal government, proposed by the Prime Minister of this country in February of 1961 at a federal-provincial conference. I say, on the contrary, that the Minister of Finance, those associated with him and the Prime Minister were met with a strike on the part of the government of Ontario, who refused to pay taxes imposed by the federal government, and this is a concession to the stand that was taken by their friend Premier Frost.

speechtext: That is nonsense.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the minister's explanation of

this very interesting legislation which he described, I think, as an act of generosity on the part of the government, and I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in which he discounted that generosity. He implied that there are other motives for the introduction of this resolution, and I suppose that in every sense of the word he considers it expedient. That is a lovely term that we use in the introduction of resolutions.
However, we are not sufficiently informed on this question at the present time to speak with confidence and therefore the members of this group intend to reserve their remarks until they have had an opportunity to read the bill.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CERTAIN PROVINCIAL TAXES AND FEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it does seem to me that before we can accept the resolution we need a little more information than the minister has given us about the background of this matter. Some of us have had quite a long experience of federal-provincial financial negotiations-the Minister of Finance has had a pretty bitter experience of them-and we do know this, that it is a rare enough thing for ministers of finance or even prime ministers simply to hand something as a concession to the provinces unless there is some historical background for it.
We all know, of course, that immense, almost encyclopedic knowledge of finance that is possessed by the Prime Minister who made this offer, and I think the minister should disclose just a little bit-lift the curtain a little bit-of that background for us and tell us why this particular concession should suddenly have been decided upon.
I think the minister should also tell us how the provinces are apt to benefit from this relatively, and if it will not turn out that this is no concession at all to the provinces that most need bolstering up financially, and that the bulk of any advantage that will come from this will be, as everything seems to be that is done by this government, to that province which financially is in the best position. I think perhaps the minister might give us a breakdown, as well as a little historical background.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CERTAIN PROVINCIAL TAXES AND FEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I gave the essentials of the historical background. This matter was discussed at the dominion-provincial conference, to which I have made reference. The provinces, of course, were interested in receiving some opportunity of levying their commodity taxes on federal crown corporations. There was some discussion as to whether in seeking something approaching equality of treatment of crown corporations federal and provincial, in respect

Crown Corporations
of taxes provincial and federal respectively the expedient should take the form of mutual immunity or mutual taxation.
The view of the federal government was that the sounder course was mutual taxation, and this view has been accepted and it is embodied in the present bill.
I indicated in my earlier statement the difficulty of making any precise reckoning of what this will mean in the payment of taxes by these 28 crown corporations.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CERTAIN PROVINCIAL TAXES AND FEES
speechtext: You must have made an estimate.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CERTAIN PROVINCIAL TAXES AND FEES
speechtext: I did, and I referred to it in my statement. I am sorry the hon. member did not follow what I said on that point. But I am not in a position to make any breakdown on this as among the 10 provinces. No one can do that at this time.

-but overnight I am confident that the Minister of Finance will consult his colleague the Minister of National Revenue and will be able to inform this committee when it next assembles whether or not there are now any outstanding claims on the part of the federal government against any crown corporation such as exists in my own province, let alone the other nine provinces. I refer to the Ontario hydro. Had the Ontario hydro any outstanding liabilities to the federal government prior to the passing of this legislation; and if so, how much, and for how long has the Ontario hydro been neglectful of its obligation to pay what might be in the opinion of the Minister of Finance a due debt under our Excise Tax Act?
Perhaps there are some other obligations of crown corporations in other provinces. Could we have, before we reassemble, a statement from the Minister of Finance as to any claims that the federal government has been advancing up to this time against crown corporations incorporated under provincial jurisdiction? Could we know what those crown corporations are, what the taxes are that have been asked for and have not been paid, and for how long have those debts claimed by the federal government remained unpaid?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I wonder if the house leader could, if possible, indicate in a general way what the business will be for the rest of the week.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, we will commence with the second reading of the bill to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, then second reading of the bill to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, followed by the committee stage of Bill No. C-67 dealing with a proposed railway line in the Gaspe peninsula. The fourth item would be the resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance dealing with crown corporations; item 5, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance dealing with the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act. The next item would be the resolution in the name of the Secretary of State dealing with the universal copyright convention.
The work for the balance of the week depends upon the progress we make in connection with this legislation.
